# Performance Night Costume Brief

Fictional evaluation document. Scope: costume administration for the 2027 policy year. Effective dates are supplied separately in the corpus manifest. This document must be read alongside other selected sources when the question names another office or location.

## Deposit amount

The performance night costume brief requires a costume security deposit of AUD 80 per outfit.

Wardrobe hire and backstage handling are related but distinct responsibilities. An outfit deposit is security held against the issued pieces; it is not an ordinary cleaning charge. If two current documents disagree, staff retain both statements for review. For this section the desk records the request under COSTUME-2027-01. The reference groups correspondence; it does not change the deadline or amount stated above. A correction must preserve the original entry and record the reason for the change.

## Cross-service boundary

This costume document does not grant authority over unrelated activities. A staff member should distinguish the stated rule from a future booking, payment, or discretionary approval. A family may ask several questions in one message; answerable portions should cite the relevant source while missing facts remain unresolved. An unanswered detail must not be inferred from an adjacent fee, deadline, room number, or event identifier. In particular, general guidance about outfit identifiers, accessory counts, and return receipts is not a substitute for an explicit rule about a different programme.

## Handling incomplete requests

When a costume request omits the student, location, policy year, or relevant date, the desk records the missing information and asks for it. The original wording is preserved in the working notes. Staff avoid copying identity documents into teaching chat or broad distribution lists. A later clarification supplements rather than overwrites the request. This distinction matters when a performer returns several pieces from a hired outfit. A response acknowledging receipt is administrative correspondence and should not be represented as approval of an exception.

## Audit example and non-equivalence

The reviewer reconstructs the event from outfit identifiers, accessory counts, and return receipts. For example, an entered reference code may identify correspondence without proving that money moved, a class place was reserved, or a consent decision changed. The reviewer compares the dated source with the actual record and records unresolved inconsistencies. Similar words across offices are not proof of identical policies: deposit, credit, submission, and acknowledgement each have a specific role in their own service. The desk retains source identity rather than combining conflicting numbers into a new undocumented rule.
